## Hypothesis Testing

Goal: use a dataset to decide between two options possible states of the world.

- $H_0$ (null) and $H_1$ (alternative) define two distributions (or classes of distributions)
- A **test statistic** $T = T(X_1, \ldots, X_n)$: one number summarizing the evidence against the null.
- A **rejection region** $\mathcal{R}$: the values of $T$ that make us reject.

The decision is a Bernoulli random variable, so everything we want to know about the test is a **probability**.

## Two ways to be wrong

| | $H_0$ true | $H_1$ true |
|---|---|---|
| reject | **Type I error** ($\alpha$) | correct ($1 - \beta$, the **power**) |
| do not reject | correct ($1 - \alpha$) | **Type II error** ($\beta$) |

- You **set** $\alpha$. Fix the size you will tolerate, then take all the power you can get.
- "Do not reject" is **not** "accept $H_0$" --- a test with no power fails to reject anything.

## MC estimates of size and power

$$\alpha = \E{\ind(T \in \mathcal{R}) \mid H_0}, \qquad
\text{power}(\theta_1) = \E{\ind(T \in \mathcal{R}) \mid \theta_1}$$

```{r eval=FALSE}
null <- replicate(k, T(rmodel(n, theta_0)))
alt <- replicate(k, T(rmodel(n, theta_1)))
# plot to determine rejection region,
# write function `is_in_R()` returns TRUE/FALSE
mean(is_in_R(null)) # size
mean(is_in_R(alt))  # the power
```

## $p$-values

- One sided:
$$\hat p = \frac{1 + \#\{T_b \ge t_{\text{obs}}\}}{B + 1} \qquad \texttt{mean(c(t\_obs, null\_dist) >= t\_obs)}$$

- Two sided:
$$\hat p = 2 \min\left\{ P(T \le t_{\text{obs}}), \; P(T \ge t_{\text{obs}}) \right\}, \text{ capped at } 1$$
- More generally, order rejection regions largest to smallest, find $\alpha$ of first rejection region to include observed value.

## Inverting a test gives an interval

Hold the data fixed and ask which hypotheses not rejected:
$$\text{CI}_{1-\alpha} = \{\theta_0 : \text{the level-}\alpha\text{ test of } H_0: \theta = \theta_0 \text{ does not reject}\}$$

- One simulated null distribution **per candidate $\theta_0$** on a grid; keep the ones you cannot reject.
- The proof is just the size of the test: if $\theta$ is the truth, the test rejects it with probability $\alpha$, so the set contains it with probability $1 - \alpha$.
